Upgrading your extension package

Source: vignettes/upgrading-extension-packages.qmd

This article is for the maintainer of an existing mizer extension package — mizerShelf, mizerMR, mizerStarvation, therMizer or your own — bringing it up to date with a newer mizer. It has two halves:

  • Part 1 is the one-off migration to mizer’s S3 architecture and simplified extension mechanism (mizer 3.4). Every package written against mizer 3.3 or earlier needs it.
  • Part 2 collects the other mizer changes that land specifically on extension code — methods that no longer dispatch, workarounds that can be dropped, tests that now fail. These are release-by-release and each one is independent of the S3 migration.

It covers only what is specific to being an extension.

Before you start: is this an extension?

Not every package that depends on mizer is a mizer extension, and only an extension needs this article. Look for any of these:

  • setClass() declaring a marker class, or .onLoad() calling registerExtension() / registerExtensions()
  • methods on mizer’s own generics — project.myClass, setParams.myClass, steadySingleSpecies.myClass
  • a rate function installed with setRateFunction(), or a component registered with setComponent()

A package with none of them — one that only calls mizer, however extensively, like mizerExperimental — is ordinary user code in a package wrapper. The Upgrading your mizer code article covers it in full, including its “If your code is a package” section. Stop here and use that.

Everything in this article is in addition to that skill, not instead of it. Work through the Upgrading your mizer code article first — its code-pattern index for the asymptomatic changes, its symptom index for anything that broke, and its package section for the version floor, the changelog, the docs and the test suite. Then come back here for what only an extension has to do. For what the finished package should look like, rather than how to get there, read the guide to creating a mizer extension package: this article does not repeat its rules, and its checklist for package authors is the acceptance test for a migrated package.

Part 1 — the S3 extension mechanism

What changed in mizer

Starting with mizer 3.3.0.9000 / 3.4:

  1. MizerParams and MizerSim are S3 classes. They are stored as lists with class vectors c("MizerParams") and c("MizerSim").
  2. S3 extension classes: an extension package prepends its class name to the S3 class vector — c("mizerShelf", "MizerParams") for params, and c("mizerShelfSim", "MizerSim") for simulations.
  3. Session registration is obsolete: registerExtension() and the dynamic S4 marker classes created at package load time have been removed.
  4. No .onLoad hook or active bindings needed: bundled datasets saved as S3 objects retain their class vectors and extension metadata under standard R lazy-loading.
  5. Extension tracking via recordExtension(): the extension requirement and package version are recorded in params$extensions (or params@extensions).
  6. Class coercion via coerceToExtensionClass(): it reads params$extensions and sets the S3 class vector accordingly. project() automatically coerces its MizerSim output to the corresponding …Sim extension class.

Step by step

1. Clean up R/<pkgname>-package.R

Remove .onLoad() entirely (and delete R/zzz.R if it held only .onLoad()), or the registerExtension() and makeActiveBinding() calls within it if it does anything else.

  • Remove registerExtension(): session registration is no longer used.
  • Remove makeActiveBinding(): datasets in data/ now carry their S3 class directly.
  • Remove @importFrom methods is: replace is(x, "MizerParams") in code with inherits(x, "MizerParams").
  • Remove deleted files from Collate:: if DESCRIPTION has a manual Collate: field, remove zzz.R (or whichever file held .onLoad()) from it.
# BEFORE:
.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
    mizer::registerExtension(pkgname, requirement = "sizespectrum/myExtension")
    if (exists("my_params", envir = asNamespace(pkgname), inherits = FALSE)) {
        ns <- asNamespace(pkgname)
        raw <- get("my_params", envir = ns)
        makeActiveBinding("my_params",
                          fun = function() mizer::coerceToExtensionClass(raw),
                          env = ns)
    }
}

# AFTER:
# Delete .onLoad() completely if there are no other load actions.

2. Delete every marker class declaration

An extension class is now an ordinary entry in the object’s S3 class vector, so nothing has to be declared. Delete

setClass("myExtension", contains = "MizerParams")
setClass("myExtensionSim", contains = "MizerSim")

and, if the package carried the workaround for the marker classes being wiped by rm(list = ls()) or by the cleanEx() that R CMD check runs before every example, delete that too:

setClass("myExtension", contains = "MizerParams", where = globalenv())

Both are actively harmful now: a sealed S4 class of the same name cannot be re-parented, which is what prevented two independently developed extensions from being chained in either load order.

Then check NAMESPACE and the roxygen comments for @exportClass, @importClassesFrom mizer and setValidity() on those names, and remove those as well. devtools::document() will not drop a stale exportClasses() line while the setClass() is still there.

3. Update the class documentation

Rewrite the roxygen block that documented the extension class:

#' myExtension extension classes
#'
#' S3 extension classes for [MizerParams] and [MizerSim] that enable S3 dispatch
#' for extension-specific methods.
#'
#' The class names are ordinary entries in the object's S3 class vector. All
#' extension-specific data lives in `other_params(params)` or in component
#' parameters (see [setComponent()]).
#'
#' Objects of class `myExtension` are created by [newMyExtensionParams()].
#' Objects of class `myExtensionSim` are returned automatically by [project()]
#' when called on a `myExtension` params object.
#'
#' No class declaration is needed. [newMyExtensionParams()] records the
#' extension on the object with [mizer::recordExtension()] and then calls
#' [mizer::coerceToExtensionClass()].
#'
#' @name myExtension-class
#' @keywords internal
NULL

4. Update constructors and setup functions

Every constructor and setup function should

  1. call recordExtension() with the package name, version and explicit requirement = "<owner>/<repo>" (now required since session registration no longer supplies it), and
  2. call coerceToExtensionClass(params), for a dispatching extension.
params <- mizer::recordExtension(
    params, "myExtension",
    version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("myExtension")),
    requirement = "sizespectrum/myExtension"
)
params <- mizer::coerceToExtensionClass(params)

For a metadata-only extension such as mizerStarvation, call recordExtension() and omit coerceToExtensionClass().

5. Migrate bundled data objects in data/

MizerParams and MizerSim objects in data/ that were stored as S4 objects have to be upgraded to S3 and re-saved. Run this once, per object:

library(mizer)
load("data/my_params.rda")

# Convert S4 to S3 list if needed
p <- mizer:::upgrade_s4_to_s3(my_params)
class(p) <- c("myExtension", "MizerParams")
p <- recordExtension(
    p, "myExtension",
    version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("myExtension")),
    requirement = "sizespectrum/myExtension"
)
p <- validParams(p)

my_params <- p
save(my_params, file = "data/my_params.rda", compress = "bzip2")

and update the documentation in R/data.R:

#' @format A [myExtension-class] object.
#'
#' The object was created with [newMyExtensionParams()] and is stored in
#' the package's `data/` directory. R's standard lazy-loading preserves its S3
#' class vector and extension metadata, so no load hook or active binding is
#' needed.

6. Replace S4 assertions and type checks

  • Replace is(x, "MizerParams") and is(x, "MizerSim") with inherits(x, "MizerParams") and inherits(x, "MizerSim").
  • In tests/testthat/, replace expect_s4_class() with expect_s3_class() throughout — for MizerParams and MizerSim as well as for your own myExtension and myExtensionSim.
  • Replace any assertions on mizer::getRegisteredExtensions() with assertions on mizer::getMetadata(params)$extensions (e.g., checking getMetadata(params)$extensions$myExtension$version and $requirement).

7. Provide an upgrade method if layout has evolved

If your extension’s internal layout has changed across versions, register an idempotent S3 method for utils::upgrade() so that older saved objects are migrated automatically when validated. See “Upgrading objects across versions of your extension” in the guide to creating a mizer extension package:

#' @exportS3Method utils::upgrade
upgrade.myExtension <- function(object, ...) {
    # Detect old layout and migrate idempotently
    object
}

8. Update DESCRIPTION

  • Remove methods from Imports: if it was there only for the S4 checks.
  • Require mizer (>= 3.3.0.9000), or mizer (>= 3.4.0) once that is released.
  • If DESCRIPTION has an explicit Collate: field, update it to remove deleted files (such as zzz.R) and include any new ones (such as upgrade.R).

9. Update vignettes, narrative docs and NEWS.md

  • Wherever a vignette describes S4 marker classes, .onLoad() or registerExtension(), replace it with S3 extension classes, recordExtension() and coerceToExtensionClass().

  • Record the change in NEWS.md:

    - Replaced obsolete session extension registration and dynamic S4 marker
  classes with mizer's simpler S3 extension mechanism. Stored parameter
  objects are now S3 objects with extension class vector
  `c("<pkg>", "MizerParams")`, removing the need for a load hook or an active
  binding.

10. Document, test and check 

devtools::document()   # updates NAMESPACE and man/*.Rd
devtools::test()       # run test suite
devtools::check()      # verify full package build and vignettes

Part 2 — other mizer changes that hit extension code

Work through these whatever the state of the S3 migration; none of them depends on it.

Working under both numerical schemes

Mizer’s numerics are no longer a single scheme. The second_order_w slot selects how the model is discretised in size — flux picks the advective reconstruction and bin_average decides whether a size-dependent factor is integrated over its bin or point-sampled at the left bin edge — and project()’s method argument selects the discretisation in time, "euler" or one of the second-order stepper "second_order", an alias for "tr_bdf2", or the superseded "predictor_corrector". Both default to the first-order choice, which is why this is easy to miss: an extension that ignores them looks correct, passes its own tests, and is then silently wrong for the user who switches them on. That user need not do it on purpose: a model created with defaults edition 3 or later is on the second-order scheme in size from the start. Aim to work under all of them, and where you cannot, say so out loud.

In size. The rules are in the guide to extending mizer, under “Respecting the model’s quadrature scheme”: build derived quantities from the rate functions rather than re-deriving them, use encounter_kernel() rather than pred_kernel() inside the convolution, write summary integrals with sizeIntegral(), and gate any array your own setter precomputes on params@second_order_w[["bin_average"]]. Two consequences reach further than that section:

  • A custom Mort or Diffusion rate must be the bin average when bin_average is on, because the transport step differences it against the bin-averaged density — getDiffusion() and getMort() already return the bin average when the flag is on, because the arrays behind them are built that way at setup, so a function that wraps them inherits it and one that builds the rate from scratch does not. A custom EGrowth stays a point value at the bin boundary under both settings: growth velocities are never bin-averaged.
  • Do not reimplement the transport step or the egg balance. They read the flux entry, so getRequiredRDD(), findSteadyState() and project() all agree about which reconstruction the model uses, and a hand-rolled copy in your package will not.

In time. The rules are in the guide to extending mizer, under “Components and the time stepper”: under either second-order stepper a component’s dynamics_fun — and a custom resource_dynamics function — is called twice per time step, once as the predictor with the start-of-step rates and once as the corrector with the midpoint rates, both times from the same t and the same start-of-step state, and only the corrector’s return value survives. What to check in code that was written before those steppers existed:

  • Be a pure function of your arguments. Compute the new state from the n_other[[component]] you were handed and return it. Anything that instead accumulates into a stored value — <<-, writing into other_params(params), a counter, a log file — runs twice per step and is wrong by a factor of two under the second-order methods while looking fine under "euler".
  • Use the rates argument; do not recompute rates from n. Rebuilding them gives the corrector the start-of-step rates again, which silently drops the whole run back to first order rather than producing a visible error.
  • Integrate your own step to second order or supply an equation. The corrector hands you midpoint values for all standard numeric rates. A custom step owns its integration: state + dt * f(state, rates) remains first order when f depends on the component’s start state. Solve the step exactly with the rates frozen, as resource_semichemostat() does, or use the optional prediction context described below. An equation-only component gets Heun integration from mizer.
  • Tolerate being called out of order. The rate functions are evaluated a second time at t + dt on the predicted state, so a rate function must not assume that time advances once per call or cache “the last t I saw”.
  • The existing rule about discontinuities still applies, and is the one thing a better stepper cannot fix: a rate that jumps as a function of abundance is not rescued by "second_order".

Test all four corners. Running the package’s own fixture under both switches, rather than only on the default path, is covered in the Upgrading your mizer code article under “If your code is a package”. An extension has more to get wrong in time, so add the order check: halving dt should move the answer by roughly a quarter rather than a half.

If you cannot support one, warn. The size scheme is a property of the object, so the setup function is the place to say so:

if (isTRUE(second_order_w(params)[["bin_average"]])) {
    signal_info(
        "second_order_w",
        paste("myExtension's detritus encounter is point-sampled at the left",
              "bin edge, so this model is not second order in w."),
        level = 1, severity = "warning", unhandled = "show"
    )
}

The time stepper is chosen per call rather than stored, so there is no equally good hook. Name the limitation in the same setup-time report, and add a project.myExtension method that inspects method before NextMethod() if you want a per-call warning as well — remembering that it catches only the calls that go through project(). The steady-state finders run the dynamics through an internal stepper, so tuneSteadyState(method = "second_order") will not reach it.

Your own FFT convolutions

Some extensions evaluate an encounter rate of their own — for a second resource, a size-structured prey component, a diet split by prey group — by copying the convolution from mizerEncounter():

avail_energy <- Re(base::t(mvfft(base::t(params@ft_pred_kernel_e) *
                                     mvfft(base::t(prey)),
                                 inverse = TRUE))) / length(params@w_full)
avail_energy <- avail_energy[, idx_sp, drop = FALSE]

That convolution is circular: the part of a small predator’s kernel that reaches below the smallest size min_w_pp wraps around and picks up the largest fish at the top of the grid (mizer issue #618). From defaults edition 3, mizer stores the Fourier-transformed kernels ft_pred_kernel_e, ft_pred_kernel_p and ft_pred_kernel_d on a zero-padded grid that is longer than w_full, so for a model of that edition the code above fails with “non-conformable arrays”. For a model of edition 1 or 2 the kernels keep their old length and the code still runs, so the failure only shows up once a user works with an edition-3 model. Replace it with convolve_pred_kernel(), which reads the length of the grid from the kernels and pads the input to match:

avail_energy <- convolve_pred_kernel(params, prey)

It already returns only the predator sizes in w, so the idx_sp subsetting goes. A vector prey is used for every predator species, which is what a diet split by prey group needs: call it once per prey group. For a predation rate, pass the predator densities on w with kernel = "predation"; the result is on w_full. For a model of edition 1 or 2 it gives the same circular convolution as the code it replaces, so your extension keeps the results it had for those models. It also uses the bin-integrated kernels when bin_average is on, without any code of its own. This needs mizer (>= 3.4.0.9002) in DESCRIPTION.

The diet of a changed encounter rate

getDiet() and getTrophicLevel() split the encounter rate between the food sources with the S3 generic getEncounterByPrey(), and take the total from the model’s own encounter rate, getEncounter(). If your package changes the encounter rate with a projectEncounter() method, getEncounterByPrey() does not know about the change, and the split no longer adds up to the total. Mizer then scales the contributions of all food sources in proportion and says so, with a message from getDiet(), plotDiet() or getTrophicLevel(). (Earlier versions ignored the change: the diet did not add up to what the predator consumed, and the trophic levels could be far too high.) The proportional split is exact only if your change affects all food sources equally. Even a change of the search volume does not, as soon as the model has an external encounter rate or a component with an encounter function.

Give getEncounterByPrey() a method that makes the same change as your projectEncounter() method and calls NextMethod():

#' @method projectEncounter myExtension
#' @export
projectEncounter.myExtension <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t = 0, ...) {
    params <- withMySearchVolume(params, t)
    NextMethod()
}

#' @method getEncounterByPrey myExtension
#' @export
getEncounterByPrey.myExtension <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t = 0,
                                           ...) {
    params <- withMySearchVolume(params, t)
    NextMethod()
}

If your change adds encounter of its own, a second resource for example, add it to the result of NextMethod() as a food source of its own, named in the prey dimension, rather than spreading it over the existing ones:

getEncounterByPrey.myExtension <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t = 0,
                                           ...) {
    by_prey <- NextMethod()
    extra <- myResourceEncounter(params, n_other, t)  # species x size
    dn <- dimnames(by_prey)
    dn$prey <- c(dn$prey, "My resource")
    array(c(by_prey, extra), dim = dim(by_prey) + c(0, 0, 1), dimnames = dn)
}

getDiet() then gives a column for it, and getTrophicLevel(), which only counts prey species and the resource in its numerator, treats it like the external encounter rate.

getTrophicLevel() takes from your method only how much food each prey species and the resource provide. It averages their trophic levels over prey sizes with the predation kernel stored in the model, so a change to which prey sizes are eaten reaches it only if the changed kernel is stored with setPredKernel(). If your package changes the kernel during the projection instead, for example with temperature, give getTrophicLevel() a method that stores the kernel in force at time t with setPredKernel() and calls NextMethod().

A getDiet() method of your own that exists only to account for your change to the encounter rate is no longer needed: replace it with the getEncounterByPrey() method. If it calls NextMethod() and then computes the diet itself, that call now gives the message even though its result is thrown away. getDiet() also gained a t argument, and getDiet() on a simulation passes the time of each saved step, so a method you keep must accept t, at least through ..., and pass it on. This needs mizer (>= 3.4.0.9003) in DESCRIPTION.

Methods on the renamed rate-array accessors

Seventeen accessors that read a stored parameter or rate array back out of a MizerParams object lost their get prefix: getCatchability() → catchability(), getExtMort() → ext_mort(), and so on. For a user nothing breaks — the get names are kept as aliases. For an extension they can break silently, because the get name is no longer a generic of its own: it is now bound to the same function object as the bare name (getExtMort <- ext_mort). A method registered on the get name is therefore never called.

Rename the method to the bare name. These eleven bare names are generics, so a method on them dispatches through both names:

catchability, selectivity, pred_kernel, search_vol, intake_max, metab, ext_mort, ext_encounter, maturity, repro_prop, reproduction_level

# BEFORE                          # AFTER
getExtMort.myExtension <- ...     ext_mort.myExtension <- ...

The remaining six — initial_effort, interaction_matrix, resource_dynamics, resource_level, resource_rate, resource_capacity — are plain functions with no UseMethod() call, so there is nowhere to hang a method at all. If your package relied on overriding one of them, that override is dead code: remove it and open an issue asking for the bare name to be made a generic, rather than leaving a method that looks live and is not.

A method exported with @method getExtMort myExtension still appears in NAMESPACE and still passes R CMD check, so nothing will point this out for you. Grep the package for method definitions whose name starts with get.

Methods on the steady-state finders

steady() and projectToSteady() are superseded by tuneSteadyState() and findSteadyState(), plus projectUntilSettled() for the trajectory. Unlike the accessors above, the old names are still generics with MizerParams methods, so steady.myExtension and projectToSteady.myExtension keep dispatching and nothing breaks.

But the four generics are independent: steady()’s method calls an internal worker, not tuneSteadyState(). A method on one name is not reached through the other. So:

  • to support the new names, add tuneSteadyState.myExtension and findSteadyState.myExtension; do not move the old methods;
  • keep the old methods for as long as your users may call the old names;
  • note the renamed arguments when writing the new methods: tol becomes distance_tol, t_per becomes t_check, and return_sim is gone — use projectUntilSettled() for the trajectory.

Withdrawing a species parameter column

If your package adds a species parameter column and takes it away again when the user switches the extension off, it almost certainly does that by reaching into the slot, because until mizer 3.3.1 nothing else worked:

params@species_params[["my_col"]] <- NULL   # old workaround — remove

The supported route is assignment, which also updates given_species_params() and triggers the rebuild:

species_params(params)$my_col <- NULL

A column mizer knows how to calculate comes back as a calculated value; a column of your own is gone. This needs mizer (>= 3.3.1) in DESCRIPTION. See “Taking a species parameter column away again” in the guide to creating a mizer extension package.

The gamma/f0 workaround can go

The defaults for gamma and f0 are now measured on mizer’s own reference state: a rate function registered with setRateFunction(), the ext_encounter array, and every other_encounter() contribution — a component’s encounter_fun included — are excluded from the measurement. Packages that add encounter, such as a temperature scalar or a second resource, used to see gamma and f0 drift when the model was rebuilt, and worked around it by pinning the current gamma as a given species parameter. Drop the workaround:

given_species_params(params)$gamma <- NULL

The gamma mizer then calculates describes the species’ baseline search volume, which is what a dynamic modulation is meant to modulate. Where a species genuinely has no predation encounter in the reference state — interaction_resource = 0, or a kernel that does not overlap the resource — supply gamma explicitly: mizer now raises an error naming the species instead of deriving a nonsense value from the additive contribution.

Tests that match messages or assert silence

Rephrased messages and calls that used to be quiet break tests in any package, and the sweep for them is in the Upgrading your mizer code article under “If your code is a package”. Two of them land specifically on extension code:

  • tuneSteadyState() warns when a custom resource_dynamics has no matching balance_<dynamics>() function, so a test asserting silence on a package that supplies its own resource dynamics will fail. That is the point of the change: supply the missing balance_<dynamics>() function rather than silencing it.
  • Anything the package emits itself should go through signal_info() rather than message() or warning(), so that it honours info_level and is collected with mizer’s own reports — see the guide to creating a mizer extension package, “Telling the user what your package decided”.

Links to renamed articles and skills

The cheatsheet articles became guides, and the extension material was resplit. Fix these wherever the package links them — README, vignettes, roxygen @seealso:

Old New
articles/creating-extension-packages.html articles/guide-create-extension-package.html
articles/using-extension-packages.html articles/guide-use-extension-packages.html
articles/extending-mizer.html articles/guide-extend-mizer.html
vignette("cheatsheet-…") vignette("guide-…")
the build-multispecies-model skill the guide to building a mizer model

The website redirects the old addresses, but a vignette() call in your own code or examples does not. Two of these rows are more than a rename: “Extending mizer” and “Guide: Extending mizer” merged into a single guide covering the mechanisms for changing mizer’s dynamics, while everything that only matters once you share an extension moved into the guide to creating an extension package. Prose that paraphrases the old “Creating extension packages” article should be re-read against the new one: its advice on marker classes was wrong by the end, still telling you to write setClass("myExtension", contains = "MizerParams").

Stored component definitions

From mizer 3.4.0.9004, setComponent() accepts a reusable definition list and stores the assembled choices in the model. This first preview supports the existing dynamics, encounter and mortality callbacks and plotting styles. Continue to register components through setComponent(); direct edits to the legacy callback slots do not update the stored definition. Those slots remain in use by the current runtime, including temporary overrides during tuning.

Changing a definition object in your package affects subsequent registrations, not models that have already used it. To migrate those models, call setComponent(params, component, definition = new_definition) from the package’s upgrade method. Omit initial state and component parameters to preserve each instance’s data. A replacement definition removes old optional callbacks omitted from the new list; a call without definition patches only supplied arguments.

The core upgrade creates snapshots for legacy components from their recorded callbacks and plotting styles. It does not invent support for future assessment, balancing or transformation capabilities. Keep using the version-stamp and idempotent-upgrade workflow in the guide to creating a mizer extension package.

Component equations and prediction context

From mizer 3.4.0.9005, a component can register rate_fun, dynamics_fun, or both. rate_fun returns a finite numeric derivative with the state’s dimensions and names. Without a custom step, mizer uses Euler or Heun; when both are registered, projection uses the custom step and diagnostics can use the equation. Do not expect a fish TR-BDF2 step to stabilise an explicit component equation. Keep a suitable custom step for stiff or non-numeric components.

Custom component and resource steps can accept predicted_state (a list of n, n_pp, n_other and t) and endpoint_rates. In a corrector these are the predicted endpoint, while the ordinary state arguments and t still refer to the start. In a predictor, Euler step or standalone diagnostic these optional arguments are NULL. Strict legacy signatures remain supported. All standard numeric fields of the corrector’s rates list are now midpoint values; extra extension metadata is not automatically averaged.

Declare a custom step’s integration_order only when its accuracy is known. sim@sim_params$component_integration records the actual per-component method, callback and order, with NA for an undeclared custom order. Test temporal refinement with coupled states as well as a component evolving on its own.

Callbacks may use exported package::function identifiers. The core saved-model upgrade adds equation and method metadata without executing callbacks. Existing models do not acquire equations merely because a package’s definition changed; update their stored definitions explicitly through the extension upgrade.

Registering convergence support

The assessment preview (3.4.0.9006) adds convergence_fun and role to stored component definitions and setProcess() for consumers and resource. Existing components upgrade as dynamic with no invented convergence support. Projection continues to work, but an operation requiring whole-model assessment can now report incomplete coverage or stop before solving.

Supply a convergence callback returning named quantitative rows (measure, value, tolerance, units). Values may be signed; mizer tests their absolute values against the corresponding non-negative tolerances. Different units can coexist. Provide meaningful measures for non-biomass and non-numeric states too; do not wrap a maximum relative cell rate merely to reproduce the old fallback. The callback receives the full rate context and the current state and time. Strict callbacks may accept only the context arguments they need.

For a custom resource, use setProcess(params, "resource", convergence_fun = "myResourceConvergence"). The core stores provider bindings, so a declaration cannot silently follow a different dynamics implementation. setProcess() is an explicit adoption of the current provider. When changing a component’s equation or custom step, explicitly select the convergence callback and role again if they still apply. A complete replacement definition must include all the optional capabilities it is to retain.

Use role = "prescribed" only when the state block is an input of the model. Freezing a dynamic state for one analysis instead uses explicit conditional scope. Temporary frozen callbacks do not alter the stored structural role. The built-in constant resource is recognised as a prescribed input. The stability preview adds partial masks as described below.

Update saved models through the package’s upgrade method to install these declarations. Test passing, failing and missing coverage; signed and zero-state measures; callback failures; provider replacement; and both quadrature schemes for any size integrals. The current Newton solver requires unsupported dynamic components to be explicitly fixed. A convergence callback alone does not add their states to that solver.

Declaring structural inputs and temporal support

The stability preview (3.4.0.9010) stores independent prescribed_mask_fun, autonomous and resource rate_fun capabilities. Changing one capability does not renew the provider bindings of the others. A provider replacement therefore needs explicit adoption of each declaration that still applies.

A prescribed-mask callback receives the model, with optional owner, component or process identifiers. It returns a logical mask with exactly the state’s dimensions and names and no missing entries. TRUE means the coordinate is a structural input, not an unknown in equilibrium or stability analysis. The callback describes model structure: do not infer a mask from a currently zero abundance or derivative. Partial masks require a numeric state; role = "prescribed" remains the shorthand for an entire input block.

Declare autonomous = TRUE only when the effective providers used by that state owner have no explicit time dependence. This is separate from stationary tuning support: sin(t) * x has a stationary solution at zero but a time-dependent Jacobian there. Custom reproduction contributes to the consumer equations and therefore needs the consumers’ temporal declaration. An explicit conditional exclusion removes the excluded owner’s unused dynamics, but its encounter or mortality contributions can still require temporal support.

For continuous resource stability, register rate_fun with setProcess(params, "resource", ...). It returns the actual resource derivative with the same shape as initialNResource(params) and receives the complete effective rates, current state and time. Keep a custom resource step as well when needed for projection. The built-in semichemostat, logistic and constant resource laws have exact equation adapters; mizer no longer estimates an unknown resource equation by taking a very short custom step.

This preview’s Jacobians cover consumer and resource coordinates only. Component equations and convergence callbacks do not automatically grant Jacobian support. Whole-model requests with dynamic components report missing coverage; callers must explicitly choose conditional scope to hold them fixed. Test time-dependent forcing, partial prescribed masks, zero-state invasion modes, stale bindings and unsupported drivers, as well as the supported path.

Registering tuning and reproduction support

The tuning preview (3.4.0.9007) adds stationary, equation_rates_fun and named tuning strategies to component and process definitions. Upgrade legacy models by explicitly installing your package’s declarations; the core upgrade does not infer them from a projecting or constant-looking callback. The complete contract and field examples are in the guide to extending mizer’s “Declaring tuning strategies” section.

Each strategy partitions its owned states into held and evolving states, declares permitted parameter paths and bounds, and supplies any preserved quantities and author-written balancer. Declare a no-action strategy explicitly when no parameters need adjustment. Coupled responsibilities or shared adjustable parameters require a joint strategy registered with setTuningStrategy().

Balancing must preserve the target state and every effective equation rate. Report source and loss terms independently, rather than hiding their changes inside a cancelling residual. Mizer constructs targets before invoking the balancer and verifies the returned model independently. It rejects undeclared parameter changes and has no generic optimisation fallback or repair solve. Test infeasible targets and parameter bounds, unselected species, zero states, and a deliberately invalid balancer that preserves only the net residual.

Reproduction is a process without a separate state. Register its support with setProcess(params, "reproduction", ...), including a law-specific level_fun when meaningful. The built-in law adapters apply only to their actual effective providers; a named replacement or S3 wrapper needs explicit support. In particular, a nonlinear or coupled RDI cannot inherit an assumption that RDI is proportional to erepro. A custom full-rates provider must expose the effective recruitment it supplies to projection.

balanceRDD() wraps the method chain in one verification transaction. Methods can call NextMethod() and then apply their own declared adjustments, but the final result must reproduce the effective target including additions such as immigration. Tuning pins that final assembled recruitment after the complete rate pipeline; intermediate RDI may change during balancing. Incidental calibration now calls balanceRDD() and retains the current reproduction law; reserve setBevertonHolt() for an intentional law switch.

Registering structural and scaling transformations

The transformation preview (3.4.0.9008) adds a transformations map to component and process definitions. Legacy extensions do not acquire support by having arrays whose dimensions happen to match species or size grids. Declare an updating hook or explicit no-action support for each operation the package supports; missing support stops the operation before changes.

Hooks receive a candidate with the core structural bookkeeping completed, plus the original model, operation details and ownership context. They run before dependent rate construction, initialisation and steady-state calculations. Move repairs such as a species-by-size spatial-overlap array into these hooks, so addSpecies() does not evaluate rates while that array still has old dimensions. Do not keep the same repair both in a hook and after NextMethod() returns.

The public transformation functions retain their S3 generics. A delegating method should let the coordinated hooks perform its data updates, rather than doing the same update before or after NextMethod(). A complete overriding method remains responsible for implementing the operation’s contract itself.

Use explicit species and grid mappings from details; choose how new cells are initialised. For scaling, distinguish extensive stocks from intensive quantities and non-numeric state. scaleModel() no longer multiplies arbitrary component state, and scaleRates() needs the component’s time constants and other rate parameters to transform consistently too. Update species coefficients and their recorded supplied values together where appropriate, and preserve the intended freeze status of manually supplied arrays.

Declare permitted update paths. A component’s own state and parameter subtree are its default paths; other extension-owned fields need explicit paths. Shared data require joint ownership through setTransformation(). Callback errors and undeclared changes are errors; an explicit no-action declaration must really mean the component’s existing data remain valid after the operation.

Support remains bound to the providers it was registered against. Updating an assessment, a biomass measurement or instance data does not re-adopt an old transformation or balancing declaration after a provider change. Explicitly register the affected capability family, or replace the complete definition, after checking that it supports the new provider. A bare setProcess(params, process) deliberately re-adopts the stored process contract as a whole. Reproduction-level measurement has its own binding and cannot re-enable a stale balancing strategy.

For removeSpecies(compensate = TRUE), the core adds each effective external-rate shortfall once and checks the remaining species’ growth, diffusion, total mortality and recruitment after all hooks. If your rate callback changes how those arrays enter the equations, supply the corresponding correction in a removal hook with explicit permission to update them. There is no numerical probe that guesses your callback’s response. Custom resource dynamics and other components own their compensation through the same hooks.

See “Transforming extension data with the model” in the guide to extending mizer for field names, callback context and a selective scaling example. Test add/remove/rename/ reorder/grid changes and both scaling operations. Include a dependent callback that checks dimensions when it is first invoked, missing support, hook failure, unchanged input on failure, and a saved-model round trip. Keep the public species_params<-() rule that table rows alone cannot reorder the model; use reorderSpecies() for a coordinated reorder.

Registering biomass and mortality diagnostics

The measurement preview (3.4.0.9009) adds biomass_fun and biomass_filters to component definitions. Register measurements independently of convergence: even a component with a known biomass needs its own stationarity assessment. The callback receives the current state and time and returns named numeric biomasses or the richer data-frame form documented in the guide to extending mizer. Declare supported filters explicitly and return unavailable rows with reasons when a requested measurement cannot be made. Keep identifiers and plotting metadata stable across simulation times, including when a value is unavailable.

Move component discovery and biomass calculation from custom plotting methods into the getter capability. getBiomass(include = ...) supplies labels, colours and coverage to plot(); plotting should consume this result. The default stays species only. Do not make a plot discover extra components behind the getter’s back, or sum incomplete measurements with na.rm = TRUE and call that a total. Use physical-source identifiers to prevent double counting a resource exposed through more than one registration path.

For mortality plots, consume getMortByCause() and its cause metadata. Registered additive mortality contributions appear automatically with the built-in assembler. A replacement Rates or Mort provider supplies a mortality_fun on the consumers process. The callback’s complete decomposition must reproduce the effective total at every state; an incomplete report keeps its missing-support reasons. Adopting this diagnostic does not re-adopt stale tuning, convergence or transformation declarations. Remove copied mortality plot logic only after checking the extension’s intended causes and presentation against the shared getter.

Reusing built-in capability definitions

The migration preview (3.4.0.9011) adds mizerMortalityBreakdown() for an author callback to reuse the built-in terms before appending extension causes. The same full effective rates are used, and getMortByCause() checks the combined sum afterwards. Prefer this to a copied decomposition or a separate call to getRates(). Predator-specific refinement is optional and must agree with the effective aggregate; incomplete attribution never licenses inventing a cause or renormalising known terms to the total.

For a known built-in reproduction law whose semantics your extension preserves, mizerReproductionDefinition() supplies the corresponding strategies and level definition. This is an explicit reuse tool, not automatic approval of a custom RDI, RDD or complete-rate wrapper. Supply transformation declarations separately and test preserved effective recruitment after balancing.

Registering capabilities during an upgrade

Extension upgrade methods can now register capabilities through validating public setters without restarting their own migration. Remove workarounds that stamp the extension as current before the upgrade has finished. Mizer retains the old stamp during the callback, processes the chain from inside out and records success afterwards.

Finishing

Run the checklist for package authors in the guide to creating a mizer extension package against the result, and its procedure for running mizer’s test suite against your subclass if the package is a dispatching extension. A migrated package is the best case for that check, since the whole point of the migration is that mizer’s own behaviour still holds for your subclass.
